analysis.investment_thesis: Engineers India is a virtually debt-free PSU consultancy (D/E 0.01) with solid ROE of 23% and a niche expertise in hydrocarbon engineering that acts as a soft regulatory moat, but government ownership caps capital allocation quality, revenue has been flat-to-declining since FY20, and the alarming forward P/E of 20.5x versus trailing of 17.5x implies the market expects earnings to soften. I do not buy businesses expecting deterioration.
key_strengths: Zero leverage (total debt INR 22 Cr on INR 2,705 Cr equity) and a large cash/investment balance generating meaningful other income — the balance sheet is pristine
Operating margin of 28.3% is remarkable for an engineering services firm, reflecting the high intellectual capital content of consultancy versus construction
Strong EBITDA momentum in FY25 (INR 665 Cr, nearly 2x FY22 levels) suggests a possible order-book upturn tied to India's refinery and energy transition capex
key_risks: Revenue has been range-bound or declining: INR 3,237 Cr (FY20) → INR 3,088 Cr (FY25), indicating order-flow lumpiess and dependence on a narrow set of large government/PSU clients

Government promoter (51.32%) means dividends and capital allocation decisions are driven by fiscal policy, not shareholder value maximization — large special dividends in the past have periodically stripped retained earnings

FCF is highly volatile: negative in FY23 (INR -147 Cr), and OCF was only INR 109 Cr in FY25 despite strong reported profits — working capital dynamics in project businesses can destroy cash unpredictably
red_flags: Forward P/E (20.55x) higher than trailing P/E (17.5x) signals consensus expects FY26 earnings to decline — buying into a deteriorating earnings trajectory is not my style
Other income (INR 160–255 Cr annually) represents a substantial share of net profit; strip it out and the core consulting economics look weaker than reported
analysis.detailed_analysis: Engineers India has the hallmarks of a quality consulting franchise — no debt, fat margins, domain expertise that is hard to replicate — but the PSU ownership structure is the critical defect. When the government controls 51%, excess capital gets paid as special dividends at politically convenient times rather than being deployed into high-ROIC opportunities. The equity base was INR 2,406 Cr in FY20, shrank to INR 1,751 Cr by FY21 (capital returned), and has climbed back to INR 2,705 Cr — this is not Berkshire-style compounding, it is a government cash register. The business is adequate at this price but not one I would own enthusiastically.
